'''''Zero: The Biography of a Dangerous Idea''''' is a non-fiction book by American author and journalist [[Charles Seife]].<ref>{{cite book|title = Zero: The Biography of a Dangerous Idea by Charles Seife|isbn=067088457X |last1=Seife |first1=Charles |date=2000 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.foxnews.com/science/what-is-nothing-physicists-debate/|publisher=[[foxnews.com]]|title = What is nothing? Physicists debate|access-date=2015-07-14|first=Clara|last=Moskowitz|date=March 25, 2013}}</ref> The book was initially released on February 7, 2000, by Viking.

==Background==
The book offers a comprehensive look at number 0 and its controverting role as one of the great paradoxes of human thought and history since its invention by the ancient [[Babylonians]] or the [[Indian people]]. Even though zero is a fundamental idea for the modern science, initially the notion of a complete absence got a largely negative, sometimes hostile, treatment by the Western world and Greco-Roman philosophy.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/2000/01/12/the-history-of-zero/36a6a2fd-9e18-484d-ae6f-450af0340830/|work=[[washingtonpost.com]]|title=The History of Zero|access-date=2015-07-15|first=Curt |last=Suplee|date= January 12, 2000  }}</ref>

''Zero'' won the 2001 [[PEN American Center|PEN]]/Martha Albrand Award for First Nonfiction Book.

==Review==
{{blockquote|Of course, Seife's book is not a typical biography. There are no tell-all interviews with the number one or any of zero's other neighbors on the number line... Seife's book begins—of course—at Chapter Zero, with a story of how only recently a [[divide by zero error]] in its control software brought the guided missile cruiser [[USS Yorktown (CG-48)|USS ''Yorktown'']] grinding to a halt. As Seife relates, "Though it was armored against weapons, nobody had thought to defend the ''Yorktown'' from zero. It was a grave mistake." Maybe it's not the pulse-pounding drama of a [[Tom Clancy]] novel, but it's enough foreshadowing to launch Seife on an essay which begins with notches on a 30,000-year-old wolf bone and ends with the role of zero in black holes and the big bang.|[[Mathematical Association of America]]<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.maa.org/publications/maa-reviews/zero-the-biography-of-a-dangerous-idea|publisher=[[maa.org]]|title=Zero: The Biography of a Dangerous Idea by Charles Seife|access-date=2015-07-15|first=Andrew|last=Leahy|date=April 15, 2000}}</ref>}}
